surface_forms: l'homme à barbiche et à nez en colimaçon

appraisal_events.evidence: He does not believe in his own genius, showing eagerness toward worldly people and journalists "qui lui étaient bien inférieurs", simulating deference to mediocre writers to become an academician, approaching a vote-controlling duchess "avec des ruses de gentleman voleur de fourchettes"; "on entendait alterner avec les propos du vrai Bergotte ceux du Bergotte égoïste, ambitieux", and in the theatre people point him out in a box that gives "un impudent démenti" to his latest book; years later his old modest formula returns as consolation for the mediocrity of his last works.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narration steadily lowers the man behind the books: ambitious, deferential to inferiors, publicly contradicted by his own life, and eventually reduced to reassuring himself with the phrase that once served as modesty.

appraisal_events.evidence: Though a disciple in his talk, "il avait été original et créateur comme écrivain"; the severity of taste that long made him pass for a sterile chiseller of trifles "était au contraire le secret de sa force"; his vices do not prove his literature false, since great artists "se servent de leurs vices pour arriver à concevoir la règle morale de tous"; and he sits up all night with a pauper woman at a village inn and leaves money so she will not be turned out.
appraisal_events.explanation: Against the diminishment of the man, the narration defends and raises the writer — crediting his originality, converting his apparent weakness into the source of his power, and showing him capable of placing himself entirely at a sufferer's point of view.

status_effects.explanation: His standing as it is registered by others falls: he courts inferiors for votes, is overheard alternating between his true and his self-advertising voice, and is pointed out in theatre boxes as a living refutation of his own books.

The passage's own verdict rescues him: originality and force are affirmed where others saw imitation and preciosity, his vices are argued not to invalidate his work, and the inn episode grounds the "gratitudes ineffaçables" he leaves behind.

ambiguities: The passage deliberately refuses a settled verdict on the man — "Ce n'est pas ce que les uns ou les autres purent me dire qui me renseigna beaucoup sur la bonté ou la méchanceté de Bergotte" — balancing proofs of his hardness against a hidden act of charity, so neither movement should be read as cancelling the other.
